zh.title: 面對批評與毀謗（鋸喻）
zh.seo_title: 被批評、被毀謗怎麼辦？佛陀《鋸喻經》(MN 21) 的原典教法
zh.seo_description: 被人罵、被中傷、被講到氣到睡不著時，佛教怎麼看？本頁依巴利《鋸喻經》(MN 21) 原文逐段解說：他人說話的五種方式（時／非時、真／不真、柔／粗、有益／無益、慈心／瞋心）、心要如大地與恆河般不可動搖的譬喻，以及著名的「鋸喻」——即使有人用雙柄鋸把你肢解，只要對他起瞋心便非佛弟子；應學心不變、不出惡語、懷慈心而住。經末稱此為應當時常憶念的「鋸喻教誡」。
zh.question: 被人批評、毀謗、惡言相向時，佛教教我們怎麼辦？
zh.definition: 被人指著鼻子罵、在背後被中傷、或只是被人用一種居高臨下的口氣說話，第一個反應通常不是道理，是身體——胸口一緊、血往頭上衝，一句反駁的話已經到了嘴邊；就算當下忍住沒說出口，那句話也不會就此消失，半夜還會在腦子裡反覆重播，越想越氣。《鋸喻經》(MN 21) 從這裡接住我們，但給的答案比想像中嚴苛得多。佛陀說：即使是盜賊用雙柄鋸把你的四肢一段段鋸下來，只要你在那當下對他起了一絲瞋心，你就不是奉行佛陀教法的人。這不是誇飾——經文把話說得很直白，佛陀要的是「心不改變、不出惡語、懷慈心而住」，對象甚至是正在傷害你的人。這是把忍辱推到人所能想像的最極限，為日常那些遠遠不到「被鋸」程度的批評、閒話、惡言，先立一個對照的座標。在真正談到這句話之前，經文先花了不少篇幅講一件更貼近日常的事：別人到底會用哪五種方式對你說話，以及為什麼「還沒被惹到之前的溫和」根本不算數——這些鋪陳，才是鋸喻能被安放的地基。

sections.heading: 「還沒被惹到之前，誰都很溫和」——忍辱幾時才算數
paragraphs: 《鋸喻經》(Kakacūpama Sutta, MN 21) 的起頭，是一件很多人都經歷過的事：一位比丘，摩利耶頗求那，因為聽到有人說他親近的比丘尼壞話，當場就火了——憤怒、不悅，甚至鬧到要打官司。聽到有人講自己在乎的人壞話就跳起來護短，那股火氣不難懂。佛陀藉這件事，把話題從「這件事該怎麼判」轉向一個更根本的問題：不舒服的話傳到耳朵裡時，心該怎麼安放。
佛陀先戳破一個大家都在做的自我催眠：一個人「只要不悅的言語尚未觸及他，就極其溫和、極其謙遜、極其平靜」；要等到「不悅的言語真正觸及他之時」，才看得出他是不是真的溫和謙遜平靜。換句話說，沒事的時候誰都可以是好脾氣的人——那不算數。忍辱的真章，只在被戳到的那一刻才顯現。

經文後面有一則故事，把這句話演成活生生的畫面。舍衛城有位居士婦，出了名地溫和沉靜，人人都說她溫和、謙遜、平靜。她的女僕起了疑心：主人真的沒有脾氣，還是只是家務打理得順、從沒被惹過？女僕決定試探——先晚起一點，主人皺眉不語；再晚起一點，主人動怒罵人；等女僕乾脆睡到日上三竿，居士婦當場抄起門閂，往她頭上打了下去，打到頭破血流。女僕頂著傷跑去鄰居那裡告狀，於是那個溫和賢淑的名聲，一夕之間變成「兇暴、無禮、不平靜」。經文沒有替她開脫，也沒有嘲笑她，只是把事情攤開來，讓人看見：沒被惹過的平靜，撐不住一次真正的試探。

quotes.lead: 佛陀先點出一個容易被忽略的盲點：
一位居士婦，出了名地溫和：
女僕試探到底，這份溫和終於撐不住：
一夕之間，溫和賢淑的名聲全毀：

sections.heading: 不管對方是好意還是惡意——五種話，同一套修學
paragraphs: 佛陀給的清單很簡單：別人對你說話，逃不出五組對照——在對的時機，或不對的時機；說的是真話，或造謠；口氣柔和，或不留情面；出於善意，或存心傷人；懷著慈愛，或懷著怨恨。把這五組攤開來看，幾乎所有讓人不舒服的話都在裡面：主管當眾的直言、朋友背後的閒話、陌生人劈頭的辱罵、家人口不擇言的一句重話，都可以歸進這張表。
很多人聽到批評，第一反應是先辯：他說的到底對不對？是不是在造謠？佛陀完全沒有把「先分辨對錯」當成前提。這張清單的用意剛好相反：不管對方落在哪一格——就算是最糟的那一種，非時、造謠、粗暴、存心傷人、又出於怨恨——你要修的功課都一樣。經文接著就把這套功課講清楚。

quotes.lead: 他人可能以五種方式對你說話：
清單的最後兩組——有益或無益、慈心或瞋恚：

sections.heading: 無論對方怎麼說，都應如此修學
paragraphs: 面對這五種話，佛陀教的不是「看情況」，而是一句固定公式：「我們的心不會改變，也不會說出惡語；我們將悲憫其福祉、懷慈心而住，不懷瞋恨。」這句話拆開來看有三層：心先不變質，嘴巴不還口，然後更進一步——對那個讓你不舒服的人生起關懷。第三層聽起來最違反直覺，但佛陀就是這樣教的。
這份慈心不是勉強擠出來一點點，佛陀要弟子把它撐到最大：不只是對眼前這個人「以慈心遍滿他而住」，還要以他為起點，把這份慈心撐到「廣大、崇高、無量、無怨、無惱」，遍滿整個世界。被冒犯的當下，不是縮起來自我防衛，而是把心的容量撐開——撐到那句話在裡面激不起一點漣漪。這段公式在經文裡反覆出現，是整部《鋸喻經》的骨幹。

quotes.lead: 面對五種話，佛陀教的修學公式：

sections.heading: 心要像大地一樣，撼動不了
paragraphs: 光說「心不動搖」太抽象，佛陀用譬喻把它變得可以想像。第一個是大地：假設有人扛著鋤頭和籃子跑來，發誓「我要把這片大地挖到不再是地」，於是到處挖、到處撒東西、到處吐口水撒尿，一邊喊「你變成無地了！」。佛陀問比丘們：這個人真能把大地弄沒了嗎？比丘們答：不能——大地太深太廣了，那個人到頭來「只會落得一身疲憊與失望」。
同樣的邏輯佛陀一路加碼套用在別人的話上：心要練得像虛空一樣沒有東西畫得上去，像恆河一樣燒不乾，像揉得透透的軟皮袋一樣怎麼搓都搓不出聲響。這些譬喻要說的是同一件事：別人的惡言確實存在，不是要你假裝沒聽見；但對一顆夠開闊、夠沉穩的心來說，那些話撼動不了什麼——真正筋疲力竭的，反而是那個處心積慮想激怒你的人。

quotes.lead: 第一個譬喻：想把大地挖到不再是地的人：
比丘們的回答：那個人只會落得一身疲憊：

sections.heading: 鋸喻：即使被雙柄鋸鋸斷肢體
paragraphs: 這是整部經最重、也最讓人倒抽一口氣的一段。佛陀說：「即使盜賊、下流之徒以雙柄鋸子逐一截斷肢體，在那種情況下，若有人污染了心，那人便不是奉行我教法的人。」這句話把處境推到人能想像的極限——不是被說了幾句難聽的話，而是身體正被活生生鋸開。即便如此，佛陀劃下的標準仍然只有一條：心不能被瞋恨污染。

這句話很容易被聽成「再過分的傷害都要忍下來，連生氣都不行，是自己修養不夠」——但這不是經文在講的事。佛陀守護的，是那個正在受傷害的人自己的心，不讓它在傷害之上又被瞋恨接管；這與加害者做的事該不該被制止、該不該承擔後果，是兩回事，經文完全沒有替持鋸的人開脫。佛陀接下來要弟子修的，仍然是同一套公式：「我們的心將不會改變，也不會說出惡語；我們將以悲憫利益之心安住，具慈心而無內心的瞋恚」——甚至對那個正在傷害你的人，也要「以慈心遍滿他……遍滿整個世界」。鋸喻立的不是一個「必須忍痛」的標準，而是一個「瞋恨不能奪走這顆心」的標準——用人類處境能想到最極端的情況，替日常那些遠遠不到這個程度的批評與毀謗，先立好一個對照座標。

quotes.lead: 全經最震撼的一句——即使被雙柄鋸鋸斷肢體：
即使對象是正在傷害你的人，仍要修這一段：

sections.heading: 「鋸喻教誡」：時常憶念，長久利益安樂
paragraphs: 說完鋸喻，佛陀給了這段教法一個名字，也給了一個很具體的練習方法：「你們應當時常憶念這個鋸喻教誡。」接著他反問弟子，把這個教誡放在心上之後，「你們是否看見任何細微或粗大的言說之道」是自己無法忍受、守不住的？比丘們答：沒有——意思是，只要真的把鋸喻放在心上，再重的話都撐得住。
佛陀最後叮囑：「因此，比丘們，你們應當將這含有鋸子譬喻的教誡放在心上……那將長久地對你們有益。」這裡有兩個重點：這段教法有正式名字——「鋸喻教誡」，經文本身也題名《鋸子譬喻經》；而且它不是聽一次就過去的道理，是要「時常憶念」、一再放回心上的日常功課。對正被一句重話纏住、翻來覆去睡不著的人來說，這正是一個可以反覆回來提醒自己的定心之錨——連鋸子都動搖不了的心，眼前這句話，又能奪走多少？

quotes.lead: 佛陀給這段教法命名，並反問弟子：
最後的叮囑：時常放在心上，長久有益：

zh.mahayana_note: 《鋸喻經》所教的「即使被鋸也不使心生瞋、反住於慈」，在後世大乘佛教中發展為「忍辱波羅蜜」（kṣānti-pāramitā，六度之一）的重要依據；大乘經論常以「割截身體而不生瞋」描述菩薩的忍辱，與本經的鋸喻高度呼應，並將之連結到「無生法忍」等更進一步的教理開展。這些是後世的詮釋與發展；本頁僅呈現巴利《鋸喻經》中的用語與教說本身（心不變、不惡口、住於慈、遍滿慈心），不對各系詮釋作裁決。

faq.q: 被人毀謗、批評時，佛教怎麼看該怎麼辦？
faq.a: 被講到胸口一緊、很想立刻反擊，是再正常不過的反應。但依《鋸喻經》(MN 21)，佛陀不要你先去分辨對方說的是不是實話、有沒有道理才決定生不生氣。他把他人的話分成五種（適時／非時、真實／不實、柔和／粗暴、有益／無益、慈心／瞋恚），然後說：無論對方屬於哪一種，你要修學的功課都一樣——「心不改變、不說惡語、懷慈心而住、不懷瞋恨」，甚至主動以慈心遍滿對方與整個世界。重點從「別人說了什麼」轉向「被觸犯時我的心怎麼回應」。
《鋸喻經》(Kakacūpama Sutta, MN 21) 是《中部》的一部經。它由一位比丘因別人說壞話就發怒的事件起頭，佛陀藉此教導：真正的溫和要在被冒犯時才見真章；他人說話有五種方式；面對任何一種都應修學「心不變、不惡口、住於慈」；並用大地、虛空、恆河、柔軟皮袋等譬喻說明心量要大到不可撼動。全經的高潮是「鋸喻」——即使被雙柄鋸鋸斷肢體也不讓心生瞋，經末佛陀稱之為應當時常憶念的「鋸喻教誡」。

faq.q: 「即使被鋸也不能生氣」是不是要人一味隱忍、活該被欺負？
faq.a: 不是。這句話守護的是受傷害的那個人自己的心，不讓瞋恨在傷害之上再多添一層傷害，而不是替加害者開脫，也不是說被欺負是活該。經文要求的是兩件事：口上「不說惡語」，心上「不被瞋恨污染」並「主動生起慈心」——把心量修到像大地、恆河那樣廣大沉穩，讓惡言在裡面激不起波瀾。這是一個極高的修行標準（佛陀刻意用「被鋸」這種極端情境來立標竿），本頁如實呈現、不淡化也不加碼。它描述的是一種透過長期修學養成的開闊心，而不是咬牙硬忍或替傷害合理化。

faq.q: 怎麼樣才能不被別人的話影響？
faq.a: 《鋸喻經》給的方法有兩個層面。一是心態的訓練：反覆修學「心不變、不惡口、住慈、以慈心遍滿對方與整個世界」這段公式，把心量養到「廣大、崇高、無量、無怨、無惱」，像大地一樣撼動不了。二是憶念的功夫：佛陀要弟子「時常憶念這個鋸喻教誡」、把它放在心上，說這樣做「將長久地對你們有益」。也就是說，這不是一次性的道理，而是要一再回來提醒自己的日常練習。

faq.q: 為什麼順境時看不出一個人有沒有修養？
faq.a: 《鋸喻經》直接點出這一點：一個人「只要不悅的言語尚未觸及他，就極其溫和、極其謙遜、極其平靜」；要等到「不悅的言語真正觸及他之時」，才能真正了知他是不是溫和、謙遜、平靜。經文還講了一個故事印證這點：一位以溫和聞名的居士婦，女僕試探到第三次，她便抄起門閂打破了女僕的頭，一夕之間名聲全毀。沒事的時候人人都像好脾氣，真正的忍辱與修養，要在被批評、被冒犯的那一刻才顯現出來。

en.title: Facing Criticism and Slander (the Simile of the Saw)
en.seo_title: How to Deal With Criticism and Slander? The Buddha's Simile of the Saw (MN 21)
en.seo_description: When people speak harshly, insult, or slander you, what does Buddhism teach? Based on the Pali Simile of the Saw (MN 21): the five ways others speak (timely/untimely, true/false, gentle/harsh, beneficial/harmful, with love/with hate), similes of a mind unshakeable as the earth and the Ganges, and the famous simile of the saw—even if bandits sever your limbs with a two-handled saw, one whose mind is corrupted is not a follower of the Buddha's teaching. The training: an unchanged mind, no harsh words, abiding in loving-kindness. The Buddha calls this the "exhortation of the simile of the saw."
en.question: When people criticize, slander, or speak harshly to me, what does Buddhism teach me to do?
en.definition: The Simile of the Saw (MN 21) teaches that others may speak to you in five ways—at the right time or the wrong time, truly or falsely, gently or harshly, beneficially or harmfully, with a mind of loving-kindness or with inner hate. But whichever way they speak, the Buddha instructs his disciples to train thus: "Our minds will remain unaffected, and we shall utter no evil words; we shall abide compassionate for their welfare, with a mind of loving-kindness, without inner hate." This standard is pushed to the extreme: even if bandits were to sever your limbs one by one with a two-handled saw, whoever lets his mind be corrupted is not a doer of the Buddha's teaching. At the close, the Buddha calls this the "exhortation of the simile of the saw," to be recollected often.

sections.heading: Patience is only proven when you are offended
paragraphs: The Simile of the Saw (Kakacūpama Sutta, MN 21) begins with a very ordinary incident: a monk named Phagguna became angry, displeased, and even started disputes because others spoke ill of the nuns he associated with. Using this occasion, the Buddha turns the discussion to a more universal problem—how to hold the mind steady when someone's words make us uncomfortable.

The Buddha first points out a blind spot that is easily missed: a person "is very gentle, very humble, very peaceful only so long as disagreeable words do not touch him"; it is only when "disagreeable words actually touch him" that we can truly judge whether he is gentle, humble, and peaceful. In other words, anyone looks even-tempered when things go their way; the real test of patience appears only at the moment one is criticized or offended. This one line sets the key for the whole discourse: what matters is not what others say, but how your mind responds when you are touched.

sections.heading: The five ways others may speak
paragraphs: The Buddha lays out a clear list: when others speak to you, their speech may fall into five pairs—at the right time or the wrong time; with what is true or what is false; gently or harshly; with what is beneficial or what is harmful; with a mind of loving-kindness or with inner hate. These five pairs (timely/untimely, true/false, gentle/harsh, beneficial/harmful, loving/hateful) cover nearly every kind of words we might meet: well-meant advice, malicious slander, harsh insults to your face, defamation behind your back—all are included.

Notably, the Buddha does not ask his disciples to first work out "whether what the other person says is true or has a point" before deciding whether to get angry. The purpose of the list is precisely the opposite: whichever category the other person falls into—even the very worst end of it, untimely, false, harsh, harmful, and born of hate—the training you undertake is the same. The text then gives that training.

sections.heading: Whatever they say, train in this way
paragraphs: Facing these five kinds of speech, the response the Buddha teaches is a fixed training formula: "Our minds will remain unaffected, and we shall utter no evil words; we shall abide compassionate for their welfare, with a mind of loving-kindness, without inner hate." There are three layers here: first, the inner mind does not waver or turn sour because of the other's words; second, the outward speech does not return harshness with harshness; third, going further, one actively arouses care and goodwill toward that person.

And the Buddha opens the scope of the mind very wide: not only "abiding pervading that very person with a mind imbued with loving-kindness," but, taking him as the object, "abiding pervading the entire world with a mind imbued with loving-kindness—vast, exalted, measureless, without hostility, without ill-will." That is, the moment you are offended is not a moment to shrink into defensiveness, but to open the mind to boundless size—so large that the other's words raise no ripple within it. This formula recurs again and again in the discourse and is the core teaching of the whole Simile of the Saw.

sections.heading: A mind unshakeable as the earth
paragraphs: To make "an unwavering mind" concrete and tangible, the Buddha strings together several similes. The first is the great earth: suppose a man came with a hoe and a basket and declared, "I will make this great earth to be without earth," and then dug here and there, scattered here and there, spat and urinated here and there, saying, "Be without earth, be without earth!" The Buddha asks: could that man make the earth to be without earth? The monks reply: no—because the great earth is deep and immeasurable, not easily made without earth; that man "would only reap a share of weariness and disappointment."

The Buddha then applies the same point to the words of others, layering it higher and higher: train the mind to be like space on which nothing can be drawn, like the Ganges that cannot be dried up, like a well-kneaded, supple leather bag that cannot be made to rustle. What these similes share is this: the external condition (another's harsh words) is not that it does not exist, but that against a mind vast and steady enough, it can shake nothing; the one truly exhausted is rather the person set on provoking you. The direction of practice is to cultivate the mind's scope until it is "like the earth—vast, exalted, measureless, without hostility, without ill-will."

sections.heading: The simile of the saw: even if your limbs are severed
paragraphs: Here comes the most famous—and most striking—passage of the discourse. The Buddha says: "Even if bandits, low men, were to sever you limb by limb with a two-handled saw, one who gave rise to a corrupted mind on that account would not be a doer of my teaching." This is a hypothesis pushed to the very limit of the human situation—not being scolded a few times, but the body being sawn open; even so, the standard the Buddha states remains "let the mind not be corrupted by hate."

This is a teaching of tremendous weight and an exceptionally high standard, presented here as it stands, neither softened nor embellished. Note that what the Buddha then asks his disciples to train in is still the same formula: "Our minds will remain unaffected, and we shall utter no evil words; we shall abide compassionate for their welfare, with a mind of loving-kindness, without inner hate," and toward that aggressor too, "abiding pervading him... and the entire world with a mind imbued with loving-kindness." The simile of the saw is not about numbly enduring pain; it sets "not letting hate corrupt the mind, and meeting the other with loving-kindness instead" against the most extreme situation imaginable in order to set the benchmark—if it is to be kept even then, how much more so in the everyday matter of being criticized or slandered.

sections.heading: The "exhortation of the simile of the saw": recollect it often, for lasting welfare
paragraphs: Having given the simile of the saw, the Buddha names this teaching and gives a method of practice: "You should attend often to this exhortation of the simile of the saw." He then asks his disciples: once this exhortation is kept in mind, "do you see any course of speech, subtle or gross," that you could not endure, that you could not hold to? The monks answer: none—meaning that if the simile of the saw is truly kept in mind, even the heaviest words can be borne.

The Buddha closes with this charge: "Therefore, monks, you should attend often to this exhortation of the simile of the saw... that will be for your welfare and happiness for a long time." Two things stand out here: first, this teaching has a formal name—the "exhortation of the simile of the saw," and the discourse itself is titled the "Simile of the Saw"; second, it is not something merely heard once, but a daily practice to be "attended to often" and kept in mind again and again, because what it yields is lasting welfare and happiness. For anyone today whose mind churns at being criticized or slandered, this is precisely an anchor of steadiness to return to and remind oneself of, over and over.

en.mahayana_note: The teaching of MN 21—that even while being sawn one does not let the mind give rise to hate, but abides in loving-kindness—became an important basis in later Mahāyāna Buddhism for the "perfection of patience" (kṣānti-pāramitā, one of the six perfections). Mahāyāna scriptures and treatises often describe the bodhisattva's patience as "having the body cut apart without giving rise to hate," strongly echoing this discourse's simile of the saw, and connect it to further doctrinal developments such as the "patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena" (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti). These are later interpretations and developments; this page presents only the wording and teaching found in the Pali Simile of the Saw itself (an unchanged mind, no harsh words, abiding in loving-kindness, pervading with a mind of loving-kindness), and does not adjudicate among the various traditions' readings.

faq.q: When I am slandered or criticized, how does Buddhism say I should respond?
faq.a: According to the Simile of the Saw (MN 21), the Buddha does not ask you to first work out whether the other person's words are true or reasonable before deciding whether to get angry. He sorts others' speech into five kinds (timely/untimely, true/false, gentle/harsh, beneficial/harmful, loving/hateful), then says: whichever kind it is, the training is the same—"the mind unaffected, no evil words, abiding with loving-kindness, without inner hate," and even actively pervading that person and the whole world with a mind of loving-kindness. The focus shifts from "what others said" to "how my mind responds when I am touched."

faq.q: What is the Simile of the Saw about?
faq.a: The Simile of the Saw (Kakacūpama Sutta, MN 21) is a discourse in the Middle Length Collection. It opens with the incident of a monk who grew angry when others spoke ill, and the Buddha uses it to teach: true gentleness is proven only when one is offended; others may speak in five ways; whichever way they speak, one should train in "an unaffected mind, no harsh words, abiding in loving-kindness"; and he uses similes of the earth, space, the Ganges, and a supple leather bag to show that the mind's scope should be so vast it cannot be shaken. The climax is the simile of the saw—not letting the mind give rise to hate even while being severed limb by limb with a two-handled saw—which the Buddha calls the "exhortation of the simile of the saw," to be recollected often.

faq.q: Does "not even getting angry while being sawn" mean forcing yourself to suppress your emotions?
faq.a: The teaching is not suppression but a change in the state of the mind. It asks for more than "not talking back" (no evil words); it asks that "the mind not be corrupted by hate" and that one "actively arouse loving-kindness," cultivating the mind's scope until it is as vast and steady as the earth or the Ganges, so that harsh words raise no ripple within it. This is an extremely high standard of practice (the Buddha deliberately uses the extreme case of "being sawn" to set the benchmark), presented here as it stands, neither softened nor embellished. It describes an expansive mind cultivated through long training, not gritted-teeth endurance.

faq.q: How can I stop being affected by what other people say?
faq.a: The Simile of the Saw offers a method on two levels. One is training of attitude: repeatedly train in the formula "the mind unaffected, no evil words, abiding in loving-kindness, pervading that person and the whole world with loving-kindness," cultivating the mind's scope until it is "vast, exalted, measureless, without hostility, without ill-will"—unshakeable like the earth. The other is the work of recollection: the Buddha tells his disciples to "attend often to this exhortation of the simile of the saw" and keep it in mind, saying this "will be for your welfare for a long time." In other words, this is not a one-time lesson but a daily practice to return to and remind oneself of again and again.

faq.q: Why can't you tell whether a person has cultivation when things are going well?
faq.a: The Simile of the Saw states this directly: a person "is very gentle, very humble, very peaceful only so long as disagreeable words do not touch him"; it is only when "disagreeable words actually touch him" that one can truly know whether he is gentle, humble, and peaceful. In favorable circumstances everyone looks even-tempered; real patience and cultivation appear only at the moment one is criticized or offended. This is also why the Buddha pulls the whole discourse's focus back from "what others said" to "how your mind responds when you are touched."
